title: Is the Rise in Cohabitation Fueling a Marriage Slowdown?
author: Delano Squires
summary: Delano Squires of the Heritage Foundation argues that premarital cohabitation is a major reason the American marriage motto has shifted from early and often to less and later. He cites Pew data showing that 77 percent of adults aged 38 to 43 have lived with an unmarried partner and compares median marriage ages and rates with 1975. Couples now move in after months of dating, which removes urgency, and the cornerstone model of marriage has given way to a capstone model after education and career goals. He points to social approval, divorced parents and religion as factors, then summarizes risks including higher divorce risk and frequent breakups of cohabiting parents. He ends by suggesting the success sequence, along with education on cohabitation risks, as a way to equip Gen Z and Gen Alpha.
points: Median first-marriage age has risen from 24 and 21 in 1975 to 31 and 28, and the married share has fallen from about 70 percent to about half.
Early cohabitation lowers the urgency to marry, shifting couples from a cornerstone model to a capstone model.
Social approval of cohabitation is widespread, with religion among the few influences that slows it.
Research links cohabitation to higher divorce risk, and about two-thirds of cohabiting couples with children break up before the child turns 12.
Squires recommends teaching the success sequence together with the risks of cohabitation.
quotes: The median age for first marriage in 1975 was 24 for a man and 21 for a woman. Today it is 31 and 28, respectively.

Today, it is quite common for young adults to live together after a few months of dating and without a clear path to the altar. This reduces the urgency to marry—in part because cohabitation has a different role in the modern life-and-love script.
In the “cornerstone model” of marriage, a couple’s union is the foundation of a life they build together.
But in the “capstone model” of marriage, couples wed after meeting several personal and professional goals related to education, employment, and economic security.
Nearly 80% of Americans ages 18 to 29 believe cohabitation is acceptable, even if a couple doesn’t plan to get married.
About two-thirds of cohabiting couples with children break up before their child turns 12. The comparable rate for married couples is 25 percent.
It is important for young people to know that they can virtually guarantee a life free from poverty if they finish high school, get a job, and get married before having children.
